analysis.one_liner: Creates a government office to manufacture and sell affordable drugs like insulin.
analysis.headline: Senator Warren's bill to have the government manufacture and sell drugs like insulin, naloxone, and antibiotics at a fair price was referred to committee in January 2020, never received a hearing or a single cosponsor, and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create an Office of Drug Manufacturing inside the Department of Health and Human Services that would make generic drugs itself and sell them at a fair price. It would start by publicly manufacturing insulin, naloxone (the opioid-overdose antidote), and at least three antibiotics within a year, and reach at least 25 drugs within three years. It would focus on drugs with expired patents that are sold by only a few companies, have had big price increases, or are in shortage, and it would bar former drug-company lobbyists and executives of companies under enforcement actions from running or working at the office.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay high prices for insulin, naloxone, antibiotics, and other drugs made by only a few companies, plus taxpayers, since Medicare, Medicaid, and other government programs buy at the same high prices. People who rely on drugs that are in shortage would also gain, because a public manufacturer could step in when private companies stop making a drug. Patients would benefit even if the office only competed in a small number of markets, since its presence would pressure private prices downward.

how_it_helps.text: The bill creates an Office of Drug Manufacturing at HHS whose stated purpose is to increase competition, lower prices, and address shortages in prescription drugs, and to reduce drug costs to federal and state health programs, taxpayers, and consumers.

It requires the government to begin publicly manufacturing insulin within one year, along with naloxone for community overdose response and at least three antibiotics, and to be manufacturing or contracting for at least 15 drugs within a year and at least 25 within three years.

The office would target drugs with expired patents sold by fewer than three manufacturers where prices have risen faster than inflation, drugs on the FDA shortage list, or essential medicines the Secretary finds are priced out of patients' reach, and could also manufacture hard-to-get active ingredients so other generic makers can enter the market.

The office would sell drugs at a 'fair price' set by considering patient access, costs to federal and state health programs, and manufacturing costs, and would revoke licenses sold to private companies if they raised prices above the fair price plus inflation or failed to bring the drug to market.
It would bar former registered drug-company lobbyists and former senior executives of drug makers under federal enforcement actions from leading or working at the office for six years.
Money from selling the manufactured drugs would fund the office, and the Director would report annually to Congress on access problems, manufacturing status, and effects on competition and prices.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers would fund the initial setup of a government drug-manufacturing operation (the bill authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary'), though the office would be designed to cover costs from drug sales. Pharmaceutical companies that profit from monopoly prices on off-patent drugs, insulin, naloxone, and antibiotics would lose revenue as a public competitor entered their markets, and the bill's licensing authorities could let the government take rights to manufacture drugs that companies currently control.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers initially, then brand-name drug makers

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes unlimited appropriations to stand up a federal drug-manufacturing enterprise, and while the office is supposed to recover costs from sales, taxpayers would bear the start-up risk if public manufacturing proves more expensive or slower than expected.

It would put the government in direct competition with private generic drug manufacturers, who argue a publicly backed producer with the power to acquire manufacturing rights and patent licenses under authorities like 28 U.S.C. 1498 and march-in rights could undercut private investment in generics and active ingredients.

The bill does nothing about brand-name drugs still under patent, where many of the highest prices sit; its 'applicable drug' definition is limited to drugs with expired patents and exclusivity or drugs subject to federal licensing authorities, so it addresses a narrow slice of the drug-pricing problem.

The scope is ambitious for a single new office — at least 15 drugs within one year, including insulin — and execution failures or quality problems at a public manufacturer could itself create safety or supply risks.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients, the potential upside is concrete: cheaper insulin, cheaper naloxone, relief from drug shortages, and downward pressure on prices in thin markets where a few companies have raised prices well past inflation. The costs are real but bounded — taxpayer money to launch the office, and disruption to generic manufacturers who would face a public competitor. The strongest honest objection is that the bill is a targeted fix, not a broad one: it only reaches off-patent drugs and shortage or price-gouging markets, leaving brand-name patent monopolies untouched. Whether public manufacturing could deliver drugs cheaper and as safely as private producers was never tested, because the bill never received a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, read twice, and sent to the Senate's health committee, where it sat without a hearing, a markup, or any further action until the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the Affordable Drug Manufacturing Act of 2020 in the Senate on January 8, 2020.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions — the only action ever taken on it.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor, and the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers came out ahead: a bill that would have created a public competitor in insulin, naloxone, antibiotics, and shortage-prone generic markets died without a hearing or a single cosponsor, so no company's pricing power was ever tested against a government-made alternative.

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor; no senator joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.what_they_did: As committee chairman, never scheduled the bill for consideration; the bill's only action was its referral to his committee.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers
against.what_they_did: The bill's target; no action on this bill appears in the record, but the bill would have created a public manufacturer competing directly against their pricing on off-patent drugs, insulin, naloxone, and antibiotics.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill had zero cosponsors in either party, so it never drew a recorded party split.

industries.note: The bill would have put a government manufacturer, selling at a 'fair price,' directly into markets where a few companies sell off-patent drugs — including insulin, naloxone, and antibiotics — and could take manufacturing rights through federal licensing authorities. Companies would lose monopoly-like pricing in those markets; patients would get a cheaper alternative.

industries.industry: Insulin makers (Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, Sanofi)
industries.note: The bill singled out insulin, requiring public manufacturing of insulin within one year of enactment. The three-firm insulin market, repeatedly criticized for high list prices, would have faced a government-made competitor.

industries.industry: Generic drug and active pharmaceutical ingredient suppliers
industries.note: The office could contract out manufacturing and could begin producing scarce active ingredients and then sell them to other companies, which would help smaller generic makers enter markets; at the same time, a publicly backed competitor with licensing powers could squeeze private producers' margins.

The bill would bar former registered drug-company lobbyists from leading or working at the new office for six years after ending their registration, reducing the revolving door between industry and the agency overseeing public manufacturing.
